newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's ANC rules out split with labour ally.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's ANC rules out split with labour ally.

text.p: South Africa's ruling party went on the offensive on Friday to quash rumours of a split in its alliance with the 1.9-million member Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu).

"If there are differences in the alliance...it does not mean that there is a divorce. The marriage is very much intact," African National Congress (ANC) Labour Minister Tito Mboweni told the Cape Town Press Club.

The ANC, Cosatu and the South African Communist Party went into a formal alliance to win power in the country's first all-race elections in 1994. Since then, the ANC has come under increasing fire from its partners for adopting moderate economic policies and abandoning its socialist background.

Acting ANC Secretary General Cheryl Carolus said in an interview, however, that the ruling party remained committed to its social mandate to uplift black South Africans disadvantaged under apartheid and wanted to keep its alliance strong.
"It would be dangerous if there wasn't an element of disagreement... We don't want a sweetheart union," she said.
The damage control drive was prompted by a leaked Cosatu report which some newspapers interpreted as an endorsement of left-wing calls for a new labour-based political party.
Connie September, who led the commission that drafted the report for Cosatu's annual congress next month, issued a statement denying that it recommended a split in the alliance.
Instead, she said the report recommended ties with the ANC be strengthened and that Cosatu should seek a new election pact with the ruling party for the 1999 vote.
She acknowledged, however, that some tensions existed, adding: "The commission and Cosatu are concerned about the current direction of the ANC on economic policy."
Cosatu has criticised the ANC for allowing the independent central Reserve Bank to maintain high interest rates alleged by some to be slowing growth.
The trade union federation is also at loggerheads with the government over planned legislation on basic employment standards which it says does not adequately protect the most vulnerable workers.
